name: Kamehameha I
info: Kamehameha I, also known as Kamehameha the Great, was a chief of Hawaiʻi Island who conquered the Hawaiian Islands, completed their unification in 1810 and ruled as the first king of the Kingdom of Hawaii until his death in 1819.

facts.born: Between 1736 and 1761 (c. 1736 by Samuel Kamakau's widely accepted dating), by most accounts in Ainakea, Kohala, Hawaii; son of Kekuʻiapoiwa II and Keōua Kalanikupuapa'ikalaninui, a descendant of Keawe through his mother
facts.died: May 8 or 14, 1819, at Kamakahonu, the compound he built in Kailua-Kona, where he spent his last years; his body was hidden and his resting place remains unknown
facts.role: Guardian of the war god Kūkaʻilimoku and chief of Waipiʻo Valley (from 1782); King of Hawaiʻi island (from 1791); conqueror and first ruler of the Kingdom of Hawaii (unification completed in 1810)
facts.known: conquering and uniting the Hawaiian Islands; the Battle of Nuʻuanu on Oʻahu in 1795; using Western guns, cannon and advisers; the Law of the Splintered Paddle; the peaceful agreement with Kaumualiʻi of Kauaʻi in 1810; unifying the legal system

t: Kamehameha rose from guardian of the war god Kūkaʻilimoku in 1782 to king of Hawaiʻi island in 1791, with the backing of five Kona chiefs and guns bought from British and American traders.
In 1795 he took Maui, Molokaʻi and Oʻahu with an armada of 960 war canoes and 10,000 soldiers, and in April 1810 he brought Kauaʻi into the kingdom by negotiation with its king, Kaumualiʻi.
As ruler he unified the legal system and used the products collected in taxes to promote trade with Europe and the United States, so that the islands would remain one realm after his death.
dyk: After Kamehameha died in 1819 his friends Hoapili and Hoʻolulu hid his body according to the custom called hūnākele, because of the sacred power, or mana, of a person. His final resting place remains unknown.
ev: Kamehameha is born, by most accounts in Ainakea, Kohala; sources place the birth between 1736 and 1761
On the death of his uncle Kalaniʻōpuʻu he is made guardian of the war god Kūkaʻilimoku and given the district of Waipiʻo Valley
He takes possession of the ship Fair American and, with its cannons, invades Maui and defeats Kalanikūpule at the Battle of Kepaniwai
His rival Keōua Kūʻahuʻula is killed on landing at the newly completed Puʻukoholā Heiau, and Kamehameha becomes King of Hawaiʻi island

He negotiates the peaceful unification of the islands with Kaumualiʻi, who remains tributary king of Kauaʻi
Kamehameha dies on May 8 or 14, and his body is buried in a hidden place

sections.early:
Kamehameha, known as Paiʻea at birth, was the son of Kekuʻiapoiwa II, niece of Alapainui, the usurping ruler of Hawaii Island, who had killed the two legitimate heirs of Keaweʻīkekahialiʻiokamoku during civil war. By most accounts he was born in Ainakea, Kohala. His father was Keōua Kalanikupuapa'ikalaninui. The Native Hawaiian historian Samuel Kamakau says that the Maui monarch Kahekili II adopted him at birth in the traditional, informal way called hānai, and that this is why Kahekili is often called his father; King Kalākaua dismissed such rumours as scandals born of the hatred and jealousies of later years. Keōua acknowledged him as his son, and he was in any case a descendant of Keawe through his mother.

Accounts of his birth vary, and sources place it between 1736 and 1761. Kamakau, writing in 1867, put it around 1736, during the warfare among the chiefs that followed the death of Keawe. His dating has been challenged as twenty years too early, but it was widely accepted because of the support of Abraham Fornander, who reckoned that Kamehameha was past eighty when he died. The historian Ralph Simpson Kuykendall believed the birth fell between 1748 and 1761. A date of 1758, linked to a visit of Halley's Comet, does not accord with accounts of his fighting beside his uncle Kalaniʻōpuʻu and would place his birth after his father's death.

At the time of his birth Keōua and his half-brother Kalaniʻōpuʻu were serving Alapaʻinui. Keōua died while Kamehameha was very young, and the boy was raised in the court of his uncle Kalaniʻōpuʻu.
sections.rise:
Kamehameha achieved prominence in 1782, on the death of Kalaniʻōpuʻu. The kingship passed to Kalaniʻōpuʻu's son Kīwalaʻō, while Kamehameha was given a prominent religious position as guardian of the Hawaiian god of war, Kūkaʻilimoku, and control of the district of Waipiʻo Valley. Relations between the cousins were strained after Kamehameha made a dedication to the gods instead of allowing Kīwalaʻō to do so. A further story tells that when Kamehameha was able to lift the Naha Stone he was held to be the fulfiller of a prophecy, which other ruling chiefs rejected.

He accepted the allegiance of five chiefs of the Kona district: Keʻeaumoku Pāpaʻiahiahi, Keaweaheulu Kaluaʻāpana, Kekūhaupiʻo, his teacher in war, and the twins Kameʻeiamoku and Kamanawa. Kīwalaʻō was soon defeated in the first key conflict, the Battle of Mokuʻōhai, and Kamehameha and his chiefs took over the districts of Kohala, Kona and Hāmākua on Hawaiʻi. His wife Kaʻahumanu, daughter of Keʻeaumoku, became his senior counsellor and one of Hawaiʻi's most powerful figures.

Foreign arms helped him. British and American traders sold him guns and ammunition, and Captain William Brown of the Butterworth Squadron guaranteed him gunpowder and gave him its formula. In 1790 the chief Kameʻeiamoku seized the ship Fair American and killed all but one of its crew; Kamehameha took the survivor, Isaac Davis, into protection and took possession of the ship. Davis and John Young, boatswain of the Eleanora, were treated as chiefs, given wives and settled in Hawaii, and became his advisers.
sections.deeds:
In 1790, while Kahekili II was on Oʻahu, Kamehameha's army invaded Maui with the help of Young and Davis and, using cannons from the Fair American, defeated Kahekili's son Kalanikūpule at the bloody Battle of Kepaniwai. Kahekili reconquered Maui in 1791 and tried to invade Hawaiʻi, but was defeated in a naval battle called Kepuwahaʻulaʻula near Waipiʻo. With the death of Keōua Kūʻahuʻula in 1791, Kamehameha became King of Hawaiʻi island.

Kahekili died in 1794, and a civil war followed between his son Kalanikūpule and his brother Kāʻeokūlani. Seeing an opportunity, Kamehameha set sail in 1795 with an armada of 960 war canoes and 10,000 soldiers. He quickly secured the lightly defended islands of Maui and Molokaʻi at the Battle of Kawela and landed on Oʻahu at Waiʻalae and Waikīkī. At Nuʻuanu his troops took heavy fire from cannon until two divisions climbed the Pali and seized the guns from behind. His forces killed most of Kalanikūpule's army, and over 700 men were forced over the Pali's cliff, a drop of 1,000 feet.

An attempt on Kauaʻi in the spring of 1796 failed when many canoes were lost in the Kaʻieʻie Waho channel. In April 1810 he negotiated the peaceful unification of the islands with Kaumualiʻi, who remained tributary king of Kauaʻi. As ruler he unified the legal system and used the products collected in taxes to promote trade with Europe and the United States. He also declared the Law of the Splintered Paddle: "Let every elderly person, woman, and child lie by the roadside in safety".
sections.opponents:
Kamehameha's power was won against other chiefs, and several of them died at his hands or those of his followers. His cousin Kīwalaʻō, the heir of Kalaniʻōpuʻu, was defeated at Mokuʻōhai. Keōua Kūʻahuʻula, who ruled Kaʻū and Puna, raided the west coast of Hawaii while Kamehameha was on Maui in 1790 and deposed his own uncle Keawemaʻuhili in Hilo. In 1791 Kamehameha invited him to the newly completed Puʻukoholā Heiau. As Keōua stepped ashore one of Kamehameha's chiefs threw a spear at him; by some accounts he dodged it and was cut down by musket fire.

On Oʻahu in 1795 a high-ranking commander, Kaʻiana, defected to Kalanikūpule and was killed in the fighting; Kalanikūpule was later captured and sacrificed to Kūkāʻilimoku. Kaʻiana's brother Nāmakehā then rebelled in Hilo, and Kamehameha returned to Hawaii to put the rebellion down. In 1810 the other aliʻi of his council wished to kill Kaumualiʻi, a course Kamehameha was reluctant to take; only his high priest and genealogist Kalaikuʻahulu agreed with him. The chiefs went on with a plan to poison Kaumualiʻi, and when Isaac Davis warned him, Davis was poisoned instead.

The Law of the Splintered Paddle itself began with an attack on innocent people. During a raid in 1782 Kamehameha caught his foot in a rock, and two fishermen struck him on the head with a paddle and left him for dead. When they were brought before him twelve years later he blamed himself, gave them land and set them free. Kamakau's chronology of his life has also been disputed, as inaccurate when set against the accounts of foreign visitors.
sections.last:
After the conquest of Oʻahu, Kamehameha ruled from Hawaii for six years while he consolidated his conquests and prepared a second invasion of Kauaʻi. At Hilo he commissioned a fleet of double-hulled war canoes called peleleu, 800 according to Kamakau, along with Western schooners, and stockpiled guns, cannon and ammunition. He took the fleet to Maui, where he stayed from 1802 to 1803, and to Oʻahu in late 1803 or early 1804. There a large percentage of his force was killed by the maʻi ʻokuʻu epidemic, thought to have been either cholera or bubonic plague. Kamehameha contracted the illness but survived, and the invasion was postponed; the settlement with Kaumualiʻi followed in April 1810.

He remained the holder of the war god Kūkāʻilimoku. The explorer George Vancouver noted that he worshipped his gods and wooden images in a heiau. Kamehameha told Vancouver that the gods he worshipped were gods with mana, through whom he had become supreme ruler of all the islands, and Vancouver decided against sending missionaries from England.

After about 1812 Kamehameha returned from Oahu and spent the last years of his life at Kamakahonu, a compound he built in Kailua-Kona. As was the custom of the time he had several wives and many children, though he outlived many of them. He died on May 8 or 14, 1819. His trusted friends Hoapili and Hoʻolulu hid his body according to the ancient custom called hūnākele, and his resting place remains unknown. Only his children by his highest-ranking wife, Keōpūolani, succeeded him on the throne.
sections.legacy:
Kamehameha is remembered as the conqueror and first ruler of the Kingdom of Hawaii, and he took steps to ensure that the islands remained a united realm after his death. According to Malcolm Naea Chun, Keōpūolani supported Kaʻahumanu's ending of the Kapu system as the best way to ensure that Kamehameha's children and grandchildren would rule the kingdom. The first company of the American Board of Commissioners for Foreign Missions arrived on March 30, 1820, less than a year after he died. His son Kamehameha III later asked Hoapili to show him where his father's bones lay, but Hoapili, knowing they were being followed, turned back.

The size of his family is debated, because documents recording the names of his wives were destroyed. Hiram Bingham I lists 21 wives and Mary Kawena Pukui counted 26; the authors of Kamehameha's Children Today list 30 wives and 35 children, 17 sons and 18 daughters.

He is honoured in the Hawaiian public holiday King Kamehameha I Day, first proclaimed in 1871 by his grandson King Kamehameha V. The state of Hawaii gave a statue of him to the National Statuary Hall Collection in Washington, D.C., as one of the two it is entitled to place there. A Benjamin Franklin-class ballistic missile submarine, the USS Kamehameha, was named after him, and he appears on the quarter issued in 2008 for Hawaiʻi in the 50 State quarters programme. His name has also travelled into popular culture: Akira Toriyama took it for a signature move in the series Dragon Ball, and the Apple TV series Chief of War depicts the unification of the islands under him.

summary: Kamehameha I rose from a chief of Hawaiʻi Island to conquer Maui, Molokaʻi and Oʻahu by 1795, with the help of Western guns and advisers, and brought Kauaʻi into his realm by negotiation in 1810. The first ruler of the Kingdom of Hawaii, he unified its legal system and promoted trade before his death in 1819.
references: Seth Archer, Sharks upon the Land: Colonialism, Indigenous Health, and Culture in Hawai'i, 1778–1855 (Cambridge University Press, 2018)
Stephen Desha, Kamehameha and His Warrior Kekūhaupiʻo (Kamehameha Schools Press, 2000)
Herbert Henry Gowen, The Napoleon of the Pacific: Kamehameha the Great (Fleming H. Revell Company, 1919)
John Papa ʻĪʻī, Fragments of Hawaiian History (Bishop Museum Press, 1983)
Samuel Kamakau, Ruling Chiefs of Hawaii (Kamehameha Schools Press, 1992)
notes: Birth: the article's lead gives 'c. 1736 – c. 1761'; start is 1736 (Kamakau's dating, 'widely accepted' per the article) with circa true. Kuykendall's range is 1748–1761. Death year 1819 is firm; the day is May 8 or 14.
Place of death: the article says he spent his last years at Kamakahonu in Kailua-Kona but does not say outright that he died there; the 'died' fact is worded accordingly. Cause of death is not given.
The article does not date the Battle of Mokuʻōhai, so it is not an event. It also gives no date for the unification of the legal system or for the meeting with Vancouver.
The article does not name his successor (it says only that his children through Keōpūolani succeeded him, and calls Kamehameha III his son: 'his father's bones').

Spellings follow the article, which is inconsistent: Kūkaʻilimoku / Kūkāʻilimoku, Alapainui / Alapaʻinui, Keawe Mauhili / Keawemaʻuhili, Keeaumoku / Keʻeaumoku, Hawaii / Hawaiʻi, Oahu / Oʻahu. The editor may wish to unify.

Kaʻahumanu as daughter of Keʻeaumoku: the article says 'his most political wife Kaʻahumanu and father, High Chief Keeaumoku' and calls Keʻeaumoku Pāpaʻiahiahi 'Kamehameha's father-in-law'; I read these as the same man. Doubt: check.
The article says William Brown guaranteed 'unlimited gunpowder from Qing China'; I wrote only that he guaranteed gunpowder and gave the formula.

The article's paragraph on Christianity is self-contradictory (Kamehameha 'originally wanted to bring England's religion' / 'believed that Christianity may bring mana'); only the Vancouver exchange is used.
The Olowalu Massacre (Simon Metcalfe killing over 100 Hawaiians in 1790) is not Kamehameha's act and is left out except for the capture of the Fair American that followed.

The article gives no historians' assessment of his rule and no numbers of dead for his battles other than Nuʻuanu (over 700 forced over the cliff); the legacy section therefore rests on commemorations.
The 1782 raid in which he 'attacked innocent people' is from the Law of the Splintered Paddle story; 'twelve years later' is the article's figure.
References: books about the person from the article's own bibliography sections (scripts/kinds/article-refs.js), chosen by title, in place of the draft's.
